title: Wilson's Theorem: Complete Classification for Non-Prime Moduli
description: Extends Wilson's theorem to all moduli n≥2: for composite n>4, n∣(n-1)!; for n=4, (n-1)! ≡ 2 (mod 4); for primes, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Formalizes Wilson primes (p∣(p-1)!+1 with p²), verifies 5, 13 are Wilson primes, and proves the Gauss-Wilson classification (product of units ≡ -1 iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}). 33 theorems, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Wilson's theorem (John Wilson 1770, proved by Lagrange 1773): (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) iff p is prime. The natural generalization asks: what is (n-1)! mod n for composite n? Gauss (1801) proved the complete classification of when the product of all units mod n equals -1 — this is the Gauss-Wilson theorem, characterizing cyclic unit groups. Wilson primes p (where p² | (p-1)!+1) are rare: only 5, 13, 563 are known.
overview.problemStatement: Classify (n-1)! mod n for all n≥2. Formalize Wilson primes. Prove the Gauss-Wilson classification of n where ∏units ≡ -1.
overview.text: Three cases: (1) If p is prime, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) by pairing each a with its inverse, except a = ±1. (2) If n = 4, 3! = 6 ≡ 2 (mod 4) — the unique exception. (3) If n is composite and n > 4, then n | (n-1)! because n = a·b with distinct a,b < n both appearing in (n-1)!. The Gauss-Wilson theorem: ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}.
overview.proofStrategy: Prove the three cases of Wilson's theorem directly. Define Wilson quotient and Wilson primes. Use Mathlib's isCyclic_units_iff_gaussWilson for the classification. Verify specific small cases by native_decide.
keyInsights: Composite n>4: n = a·b with a≠b, both factors appear in (n-1)!, so n | (n-1)!
n=4 is unique: the only composite n where (n-1)! is neither 0 nor -1 mod n
Wilson primes: p | (p-1)!+1 always (by Wilson); Wilson prime requires p² | it
Gauss-Wilson ↔ cyclic units: the full classification relies on Mathlib's cyclicity theorem
prerequisites: Wilson's theorem for primes: pairing inverses

conclusion.summary: Wilson's theorem fully generalized: complete classification for all n≥2, Wilson primes defined and verified (5 and 13), Gauss-Wilson classification proved. 33 theorems, 9 definitions, 688 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The only known Wilson primes are 5, 13, and 563. Whether infinitely many exist is unknown. The Gauss-Wilson classification is the number-theoretic foundation for understanding cyclic unit groups in algebraic number theory.
openQuestions: Prove Wilson prime finiteness/infinitude — a major open problem
